Abstract

Networks that matter most - defence, power grid control, classified government systems - are monitored through a data diode: hardware that lets a copy of the traffic out to a monitoring enclave and allows nothing back. A sensor in that enclave never observes replies, cannot query a reputation service, cannot probe a host and cannot block anything. Detection methods and public datasets almost universally assume two-way visibility, so a conventionally trained detector degrades sharply when deployed there. Until now, how sharply, and why, had not been measured.

This report presents EKAGRA, a streaming threat-detection sensor built for that constraint, and the experimental programme behind it. On 877,801 real flows from the corrected CIC-IDS2017 re-extraction, with a temporal split and source and destination addresses excluded, a conventional detector falls from 0.9793 to 0.6903 binary F1 when restricted to one direction. Our central finding is that the loss is not caused by the missing direction but by missing per-host state: a sensor that maintains sixteen host-window aggregates over a 60-second window scores 0.9810 on the same one-way traffic, matching full visibility. A control experiment showed those sixteen features alone reach 0.9812, which narrowed our own headline claim; a further experiment showed they collapse when attacks are slow and diffuse, which is why the shipped sensor keeps per-flow evidence alongside them.

EKAGRA covers the six threat classes named in the problem statement, attaches a severity and a conformally calibrated confidence to every alert, and abstains rather than guessing when the evidence is weak (9.11% of cases, with 99.55% accuracy on the remainder). Every alert is sealed into a SHA-256 hash chain with a per-bundle HMAC, which an analyst re-verifies inside an air-gapped browser console; seven tests attack that chain, including a full forward re-forge. The system sustains 610 to 672 Mbps on commodity hardware, holds 2.66 MB of state for 14,817 hosts, and emits alerts within 75 seconds. It passes 290 automated tests, of which several fail the build if any component in the detection path can open a network socket.

The report also sets out the commercial case: an addressable market anchored on NCIIPC's eight critical sectors, a positioning analysis against open-source IDS, commercial NDR platforms and diode vendors, an open-core business model with a five-year cost comparison, a go-to-market path through pilot deployment and government procurement, a risk register, and the compliance context created by the IT Act and CERT-In's 2022 directions.

Keywords: unidirectional network monitoring, data diode, network intrusion detection, streaming host-window features, conformal prediction, selective classification, tamper-evident evidence, JA4, QUIC, CIC-IDS2017, critical information infrastructure.

How this report is organised

The deck is six slides and the demonstration video is two minutes. Neither can carry a method, a threat model or a cost model. This report is written to be the place where those live, and it is organised so a reader can enter at the depth they need.

A NOTE ON NUMBERS

PART I

The problem and the solution

Chapter 1Introduction

1.1 Background: monitoring what you cannot talk to

A data diode is a physical one-way link. Light travels down a fibre in one direction and there is no return path at all - not a firewalled one, not a rate-limited one: none. Organisations use diodes when a network is too sensitive to risk any inbound route, but still needs to be watched. The diode copies traffic out to a monitoring enclave, and an attacker who compromises the enclave gains nothing that leads back in.

The security property is absolute, and so is its cost to detection. A sensor behind the diode sees only one side of every conversation. It never sees the SYN-ACK that would confirm a connection, the NXDOMAIN that would betray a domain-generation algorithm, the RST that reveals a closed port, or the certificate that identifies a server. It cannot enrich an observation with a reputation lookup, because the lookup is an outbound connection. It cannot verify a suspicion by probing the host. It cannot block. It observes, decides, and records - alone.

1.2 Motivation

Two things motivated this project. First, every widely used intrusion-detection dataset (CIC-IDS2017, CSE-CIC-IDS2018, UNSW-NB15) ships bidirectional flow records, and most published pipelines assume enrichment is available. A detector trained on those records and deployed behind a diode is being asked to work on inputs unlike anything it saw in training, and nobody can tell it that it is wrong, because no feedback path exists.

Second, the failure is silent. A detector starved of its usual signals does not announce that it has been blinded; it keeps emitting confident labels. In an enclave with no return path, an unchallengeable wrong answer is worse than an honest refusal to answer. That observation shaped two of this system's defining features: calibrated abstention, and evidence that can be checked independently after the fact.

1.3 Problem statement

Problem statement SIH26145, issued by the National Technical Research Organisation, asks for AI-based detection of cyber threats in unidirectional IP traffic. Its operative constraints, quoted:

"The enclave can see everything crossing the link, but it has no physical or protocol-level path back into the production network."
"Treat the input as strictly read-only. Any design that assumes a return path, a live query to the source, or an inline block is out of scope."
"TLS/QUIC sessions must be analysed from metadata only." ... "must process traffic incrementally and raise alerts with bounded latency"

It names six threat classes - volumetric and protocol denial of service, command-and-control beaconing, domain-generation algorithms and DNS tunnelling, malware inside encrypted sessions, reconnaissance and scanning, and data exfiltration - and requires each alert to carry a severity and a confidence. Appendix B maps every clause to the component that satisfies it, including the one clause we have not yet satisfied.

1.4 Research question

Stated so that it can be answered with an experiment rather than an opinion: how much detection performance does a one-way tap actually cost, and which part of the lost visibility causes the cost? The answer determines the design. If the cost comes from the missing direction itself, the only remedies are better priors or more data. If it comes from something the sensor could have kept but did not, the remedy is engineering - and the diode constraint stops being an excuse.

1.6 Scope

1.7 Contributions

  1. A measurement. The cost of one-way visibility on 877,801 real flows, with the control experiments that attribute it to per-host state rather than to direction.
  2. A sensor built to a measured visibility profile rather than to a dataset's convention, covering six threat classes in a single streaming pass.
  3. Calibrated abstention as a first-class output, with a distribution-free guarantee and per-class thresholds, for a setting where a wrong answer cannot be corrected.
  4. Evidence that survives its own author: a hash chain plus keyed HMAC, verified independently in the browser, with a stated threat model and a stated limit.
  5. A pre-registered experimental record: 42 predictions fixed before their runs, 17 refuted and published, including the claim the project was named for.

Chapter 2Existing systems and the gap

2.1 Academic work

Machine learning for network intrusion detection is a mature literature with a well-documented reproducibility problem. Sommer and Paxson's Outside the Closed World set out why the field's results so often fail to transfer to deployment: the cost of a false positive, the diversity of benign traffic, and evaluation on corpora whose structure leaks the answer. Arp and colleagues catalogued ten recurring methodological faults in security machine learning, several of which - sampling bias, spurious correlations, inappropriate baselines - we defend against explicitly in Chapter 9.

Work specific to unidirectional visibility is thin. The nearest neighbours are flow-exporter studies (what is lost when NetFlow replaces packets) and one-directional sampling work in high-speed backbones. Neither asks our question, which is what a detector should be fed when the reverse direction is structurally unavailable rather than merely sampled away.

2.2 The dataset problem, and what we did about it

CIC-IDS2017 is the most-used benchmark in this area and has documented defects. Engelen, Rimmer and Joosen re-examined the capture and found label errors and feature-extractor faults serious enough to change published conclusions; later work by Lanvin and colleagues reached compatible findings. We therefore use the corrected re-extraction published on Zenodo (record 22016274, CC-BY-4.0) rather than the original CSVs, and we make three further decisions that keep the numbers honest:

  • Source and destination IP addresses are excluded from every feature set. The testbed uses fixed attacker addresses; a model given them memorises the attacker and reports a meaningless near-perfect score. This is the single most consequential preprocessing decision in the pipeline.
  • The split is temporal, never random. CIC-IDS2017 runs Monday to Friday with different attacks on different days. A random split places flows from one attack episode on both sides of the split and leaks the answer. A temporal split means some attack classes appear only in test - which is realistic, and is why binary F1 is reported as the headline with macro F1 alongside.
  • Every one of the 103 features is classified by observability into forward-observable (35, kept), backward-derived (33, dropped) and bidirectional aggregate (35, dropped). The classification is printed by the adapter so a reviewer can dispute any single assignment, and invariants over it are pinned by tests.

THE ABLATION TRAP WE AVOIDED

A careless ablation treats Flow IAT Mean as "forward IAT with noise" and keeps it. On a one-way tap the sensor computes a different quantity over forward packets only, which this CSV does not contain. We drop such columns rather than assume them observable. Keeping them would have inflated the one-way condition and hidden the very effect we set out to measure.

2.3 Operational tools in use today

2.4 The gap, stated precisely

  • No public dataset or published pipeline is built for structurally one-way visibility.
  • The cost of that visibility had not been quantified, and its cause had not been attributed.
  • Deployed detectors rarely decline to answer. Behind a diode, an unverifiable guess carries a cost that a confident wrong label does not pay anywhere else.
  • Alert records are rarely provable. If the log can be edited afterwards, an alert is an assertion rather than evidence - which matters for both incident response and the log-retention obligations described in Chapter 16.

Chapter 3Requirements

3.1 Functional requirements

3.2 Non-functional requirements

3.3 Constraints and assumptions

  • Constraint. No component in the detection path may open a network connection. This is enforced by a test that parses every module and fails the build on a network import (Chapter 10.2).
  • Constraint. Payload bytes must never reach feature code. Protocol features are computed from handshake metadata only.
  • Assumption. The enclave is physically and administratively access-controlled, which is why the console ships without authentication. Chapter 15 records this as a risk with a mitigation rather than as a settled matter.
  • Assumption. The diode or SPAN port delivers a faithful copy of the forward direction. Packet loss in the tap itself is outside our control and is not modelled.
  • Assumption. Clocks within the enclave are consistent to within the 15-second lateness budget. Beyond that, late records are dropped and counted rather than silently reordered.

PART II

Technical design, implementation and evidence

Chapter 4System architecture

4.1 Principles

  1. One-way by construction. The package layout mirrors the data flow: detect may import from features, never the reverse, and nothing imports the ingest source except the pipeline entry point. The constraint is not a convention - a test enforces it.
  2. Train on what the tap delivers. A visibility filter sits immediately after ingest, so training data and deployment data pass through the same reduction. This is the difference between a detector that degrades in the field and one that does not.
  3. Single pass, bounded state. No global sort, no full-corpus pass, no unbounded dictionary. Memory is a function of the number of live hosts, not of traffic volume.
  4. Every output is accountable. An alert carries what was observed, which model decided, and a cryptographic link to the alert before it.

4.2 Stages and responsibilities

4.3 Technology choices and their justification

4.4 Streaming with bounded latency and bounded memory

The window is 60 seconds and the lateness budget is 15 seconds, so an alert appears at most 75 seconds after its window opens. The budget exists because a flow assembler emits records after their flows end, so records arrive out of order with respect to their own start times; several windows are therefore kept open, and anything later than the budget is dropped and counted rather than silently misplaced.

  • Cardinality (how many distinct peers or ports a host touched) uses HyperLogLog, which estimates distinct counts in fixed space.
  • Frequency (how concentrated a host's traffic is on its top peer) uses a Count-Min Sketch with Misra-Gries style heavy-hitter tracking.
  • Volume against baseline uses exponentially decayed per-host counters, so "unusual for this host" needs no stored history.
  • Exactness where it is affordable: estimators start exact and promote to sketches only above 256 distinct values, which is why 14 of 16 features are bitwise identical to an exact batch computation (exp05).

WHY THIS MATTERS OPERATIONALLY

Bounded memory is what allows the sensor to run on a commodity server in an enclave with no elastic capacity. 2.66 MB of state for 14,817 hosts means state is roughly 0.18 KB per host, so capacity planning is a multiplication rather than a gamble.

Chapter 5Detection methodology

5.1 Visibility profiling: the step most pipelines skip

Before any model is trained, the corpus is passed through the same visibility filter that a deployed sensor would sit behind. Each of CIC-IDS2017's 103 features is classified as forward-observable, backward-derived or bidirectional-aggregate, and only the first class survives. This is what the report calls visibility-matched training, and it is the difference between measuring a detector's performance and measuring a dataset's convenience.

5.2 The central finding: memory, not direction

A per-flow detector judges each connection in isolation. On a one-way tap, one connection carries little information. A host's behaviour over a minute carries a great deal, and all of it is visible from one side: how many distinct peers and ports it touched, how regular its inter-arrival times are, how concentrated its traffic is on a single destination, and how its volume compares with its own baseline.

5.3 The sixteen host-window features

Five of the ten highest-gain features in the final model come from this group: hw_dst_flows_per_src, hw_src_fanout_per_flow, hw_dst_fwd_pkts, hw_src_n_dports and hw_src_fwd_pkts. That ranking was a pre-registered prediction, and it held.

5.4 Protocol evidence without decryption

Two of the six threat classes are defined by protocol evidence that host-window aggregates deliberately ignore. Nine further features supply it, kept as a separate group so that every earlier measurement remains comparable:

  • DNS, six features. Character entropy of queried names, bigram rarity under a causal language model (the n-gram analysis the problem statement names), mean and maximum label length, digit ratio, and query count. Random-looking names indicate a domain-generation algorithm; unusually long labels indicate tunnelling.
  • TLS, three features. JA4 client fingerprint rarity, whether the fingerprint is novel for this host, and handshake count.

Three findings that only real traffic could produce

5.5 The six detector heads

READ THE SUPPORT COLUMN

The exfiltration head is evaluated on thirteen test cells and the DGA head on fifty-three. Those numbers are thin enough that the corresponding scores should be read as indicative, not as performance guarantees. We report them with their support rather than quoting the score alone.

5.6 Severity, kept separate from confidence

The obvious formula, severity = class x confidence, destroys both inputs: a near-certain port scan and a doubtful exfiltration multiply to similar numbers and demand opposite responses. CVSS separates base score from confidence and NIST SP 800-30 separates impact from likelihood; so does this system. The severity function does not accept a confidence argument, and a test asserts its signature so that nobody can quietly add one.

THE FIRST VERSION OF SEVERITY WAS WRONG, AND THE CORPUS SAID SO

Each class was originally given its own magnitude feature - ports for scanning, flows for beaconing. Measured across 90,794 logged alerts the medians came out at 0.00, because an alert fires on a host and the evidence may sit on either side of that host's cell: a scan alert fires on the host being scanned, whose source-side counters are empty by construction. Half the magnitude features were reading the wrong side and filing established beacons as low severity. The fix was to narrow the claim rather than to find a cleverer feature: volume raises severity only where volume is the damage (exfiltration, covert encrypted channels), read side-agnostically. A magnitude that reads the wrong side is worse than no magnitude, because it looks quantitative.

Chapter 6Uncertainty, calibration and abstention

6.1 Why a diode sensor must be able to decline

A detector behind a one-way link cannot ask a follow-up question. It cannot fetch the certificate, probe the port or consult a feed. When the evidence is genuinely ambiguous the only honest options are to guess or to say so. Forcing a label manufactures confidence the sensor does not have, and the analyst has no way to tell the difference between a confident correct answer and a confident invention.

6.2 Split-conformal prediction

A calibration set that the model never trained on provides nonconformity scores; the (1 - alpha) quantile of those scores becomes the threshold. The guarantee is distribution-free and finite-sample: over exchangeable data the prediction set contains the true label at least (1 - alpha) of the time, with no assumption that the model is well specified. ABSTAIN is emitted when no label clears its threshold, and it means precisely: under this sensor's visibility, the observation does not support a confident label.

6.3 Why Mondrian, and a failure along the way

A pooled conformal guarantee is satisfied almost entirely by the dominant class: at alpha = 0.10 the average coverage looks correct while the rare attack classes are quietly uncovered. Mondrian (class-conditional) conformal calibrates a separate threshold per class and fixes that. Our first Mondrian implementation abstained on 100% of everything - a calibration bug that a coverage plot made obvious immediately, and a reason the console exposes the calibration panel rather than a single accuracy number.

6.4 What abstention means for the operator

  • Abstentions are logged, not discarded. They appear in the console as a distinct state, and they are counted in the header statistics.
  • A rising abstention rate is a drift signal: it is the sensor reporting that traffic no longer resembles its calibration set, which is exactly the condition a diode deployment cannot otherwise detect.
  • An operator can tune alpha to trade coverage for volume, and the trade is explicit rather than buried in a threshold.

Chapter 7Evidence, integrity and the threat model

7.1 What an alert has to prove

An alert is only useful in an investigation if nobody could have altered it afterwards - including the operator of the sensor. Each alert is stored as a bundle: the observed feature vector, the fingerprint of the model that decided, the decision path, the calibrated confidence, the severity, and the hash of the previous bundle.

7.2 Canonicalisation: the part that is easy to get wrong

Hashing a record means hashing bytes, and the same logical record can serialise to different bytes. Four decisions make the digest stable, each pinned by a test:

  • Key order is normalised, so a dictionary that round-trips through JSON in a different order still hashes identically.
  • Floating-point values are written at fixed precision, so a value that survives a save and reload does not silently change its digest.
  • Negative zero hashes like zero, because IEEE 754 distinguishes them and arithmetic can produce either.
  • Non-finite values are rejected rather than encoded, so a NaN cannot enter the digest and make a chain unverifiable.

7.3 Threat model

7.4 Independent verification in the browser

The console does not ask the server whether the log is intact. It re-computes every SHA-256 digest itself using the Web Crypto API and re-links the chain in the browser. The server's own verdict is displayed beside the browser's. When the two disagree, that disagreement is the alarm - a property no single-implementation check can offer, and the reason the demonstration shows the two verdicts side by side.

7.5 The limit, stated

WHAT THIS DOES NOT SURVIVE

Integrity rests on a key held inside the enclave. An adversary who steals that key can rebuild a valid chain, and nothing in the current design would reveal it. There is no external anchor and no asymmetric signature yet. Chapter 19 places hardware key custody and public-key signing at priority four, and Chapter 15 carries the corresponding risk.

8.3 Algorithms worth naming

8.4 Sharding, and an honest result

Traffic is partitioned by host across worker processes so that per-host state stays local to one shard. Throughput scales sub-linearly: 35,992 packets per second on one shard, 108,938 on twelve, a speed-up of 3.03. Four pre-registered predictions about sharding were refuted in a single experiment, including our expectation that the sharded output would be bit-identical to the single-process output: 8 to 21 cells per configuration disagree, because a host's records can straddle a window boundary differently once partitioned.

8.5 The read-only API and the console

The console is a single HTML file with no framework, no CDN reference and no build step, because an enclave has no package registry and no internet. Opened directly from disk with no server at all, it falls back to a bundled snapshot so that a reviewer can inspect the evidence model without running anything.

Chapter 9Experimental programme and results

9.1 Method: pre-registration

Before an experiment's first run, its predictions are written into the experiment file. The run prints a verdict for each and persists it to results/exp*_verdicts.json. Predictions are never edited afterwards; where a prediction was badly worded, it is annotated rather than reworded. This removes the most common way results mislead, which is deciding what you expected after seeing the answer.

9.2 The headline measurement

OUR OWN CONTROL NARROWED OUR HEADLINE CLAIM

This project was originally built around a claim that a purpose-designed one-way feature set beats a retrained baseline. Condition G - sixteen host-window features and nothing else - matched the full model at 0.9812, which showed that per-host state, not our feature engineering, was doing the work. We rewrote the claim and published the control. Predictions P2, P3 and P4 are recorded as refuted in Chapter 9.7.

9.3 The stress test that narrowed it further

Real intrusions are often slow and originate from hosts that also carry ordinary traffic. Experiment 10 re-times and re-homes the same real attack flows so that they share each host-window cell with 59 to 188 times as many benign flows, leaving every per-flow feature untouched.

  • The one-way tap still costs nothing: forward-only features track or beat full visibility at every density tested (0.937 to 0.994 binary F1).
  • Host-window features alone fail. Every flow in a cell receives the same vector, so an attack outnumbered 59-to-1 inside its own cell cannot be separated from its neighbours. The condition that was best in exp04 (0.599 macro F1) is worst here (0.35 falling to 0.28).
  • The shipped configuration keeps both, which is why condition E and not condition G is what the sensor runs.

9.4 Performance

A CLAIM WE RETRACTED

An earlier version of this work claimed 1 Gbps line rate. Measurement did not support it and the claim was withdrawn; the honest figure is 610 to 672 Mbps, and our own documents once disagreed with each other about it (108,938 pkt/s in one file, 119,918 in another - throughput benchmarks move with machine load). A compiled fast path is the route to line rate and is on the roadmap, not in the measurements.

9.5 Domain-generation algorithms: the weakest class

THE MOST IMPORTANT NEGATIVE RESULT IN THIS PROJECT

A detection threshold calibrated on our own generated benign names flags 89.6% of real benign names. Generated traffic is a controlled instrument for isolating an effect; it is not a substitute for real data, and any threshold set on it is meaningless in deployment. This single number is why every operating point in this report is set on real traffic.

9.6 Every refuted prediction

Chapter 10Verification, testing and quality

10.1 Test strategy

10.2 Constraints enforced by the build

Four of this system's guarantees are architectural, and architectural guarantees decay unless something mechanical defends them:

  • A test walks the abstract syntax tree of every module in the detection path and fails the build if any network client is imported - socket, requests, urllib, httpx, aiohttp and others. This is what makes "read-only" a property rather than a promise.
  • A test fails the build if any write endpoint appears in the API surface.
  • A test asserts that the severity function's signature does not accept confidence.
  • A test checks that every value interpolated into the console's DOM is escaped, so an attacker-controlled hostname cannot become script.

10.3 Results

290tests passing
0known defects open
7integrity attacks tested
3browser engines verified

Hostile-input testing covers the parsers most exposed to attacker-controlled bytes: DNS name compression with pointer loops, truncated TLS records, and QUIC Initial packets with inconsistent length fields. The parsers reject rather than crash, which matters because in this deployment a crash is the only kind of denial of service an attacker can still cause.

PART III

The business case

Chapter 11Market and opportunity

11.1 Who is obliged to solve this problem

The buyer for this system is not a generic enterprise security team. It is an operator of infrastructure that the state has designated as critical, and whose monitoring is already constrained by a one-way boundary.

India's National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC) is a unit of NTRO - the same organisation that issued this problem statement - created under Section 70A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (as amended in 2008) and notified in January 2014. It is the national nodal agency for protecting critical information infrastructure, and it identifies these critical sectors:

11.2 The problem is growing, and it is measured

CERT-In handled 29.44 lakh cyber security incidents in 2025, an increase of about 85% over the 15.92 lakh recorded in 2023, alongside 1,530 alerts and 390 vulnerability notes; 231 audit organisations were empanelled to expand assessment capacity across critical ICT infrastructure. Incident volume of that order is what makes an analyst's time the scarce resource, and it is the reason this system treats a calibrated abstention as more valuable than an extra uncertain alert.

11.3 Market size

AN HONEST NOTE ON MARKET NUMBERS

Research firms disagree materially about the diode market: against MarketsandMarkets' $0.56B for 2026, other published estimates for adjacent definitions range from about $1.2B to $1.8B, with CAGRs from 6.6% to 15%. The spread comes from scope - whether gateways, services and software are counted. We quote one source consistently and name it, rather than selecting the largest number available.

11.4 Why now

  • Encrypted traffic has outgrown inspection. In our own capture, QUIC carried more HTTPS packets than TCP. Detection that depends on payload inspection is losing ground; metadata-based detection is the remaining lever.
  • Regulatory pressure is rising. CERT-In's 2022 directions oblige a wide class of organisations to maintain logs securely for 180 days (Chapter 16), which raises the value of evidence that can be shown to be unaltered.
  • Strategic autonomy is procurement policy, not sentiment. A detector that runs with no foreign cloud dependency and no outbound telemetry is easier to approve for a classified network than one that phones home.

Chapter 12Competitive landscape and positioning

12.1 Feature comparison

12.2 What is defensible, and what is not

POSITIONING IN ONE SENTENCE

Diode vendors move data across the boundary safely and commercial NDR detects threats where a return path exists; EKAGRA is the detection layer for the enclave on the far side of the diode, which is precisely where neither of them operates.

Chapter 13Business model, pricing and cost

13.1 Model: open core with paid assurance

The detection engine, the console and the evidence format are open and free, for three reasons that are specific to this buyer rather than ideological. A classified network cannot accept a component it is not allowed to inspect. A security claim that cannot be audited is worth less than one that can. And a zero-licence engine removes the recurring foreign-currency line item that makes commercial NDR hard to sustain across many small enclaves.

The margin sits in calibration and assurance, which is also where the customer's real risk sits: Chapter 9 shows that a threshold set on the wrong corpus flags 89.6% of benign names. Calibration is not a service invented to create revenue; it is the step that determines whether the system works at that site.

13.2 Cost of ownership

13.3 Unit economics of an enclave

  • One sensor covers one enclave. Capacity is bounded by throughput (610 to 672 Mbps today) and by host count (about 0.18 KB of state per host), so sizing is arithmetic, not guesswork.
  • A site beyond that throughput adds shards or servers; cost grows in steps of a commodity server rather than in steps of a licence tier.
  • Because there is no per-IP meter, monitoring more of the network does not increase the bill - which is the behaviour a defender wants and a per-IP licence discourages.

Chapter 14Go-to-market and deployment

14.1 Where the system physically sits

14.2 Adoption path

14.3 Route to the customer

  • Through the problem owner. NTRO issued the problem statement and NCIIPC is its unit; a pilot sponsored by the problem owner is the natural first deployment and needs no market creation.
  • Through sector regulators and CERT-In empanelment, where audit and assessment organisations already engage the same operators.
  • Through public-sector enterprises in power and transport, whose operational technology networks already contain diodes purchased for compliance reasons.
  • Through academic collaboration, because the measurement is publishable and a published result is a procurement asset in this sector.

14.4 What would make a pilot fail, and how we would know early

Chapter 15Risk register

Chapter 16Compliance, standards and intellectual property

16.1 Indian legal and regulatory context

16.2 Technical standards used

  • FIPS 180-4 for SHA-256 and RFC 2104 for HMAC: standard primitives, no bespoke cryptography.
  • RFC 9000 and RFC 9001 for QUIC and QUIC-TLS: Initial packet protection uses published keys, which is what makes metadata-only QUIC analysis legitimate rather than a decryption workaround.
  • MITRE ATT&CK for threat-stage vocabulary, so that severity weights map to a recognised kill-chain position rather than to our own taxonomy.
  • CVSS and NIST SP 800-30 for the principle that impact and likelihood are separate axes (Chapter 5.6).
  • JA4 for TLS client fingerprinting, chosen over JA3 on measured grounds.

16.3 Intellectual property and licensing

  • The implementation is our own work. Third-party dependencies are standard open-source libraries, used unmodified.
  • CIC-IDS2017 and its corrected re-extraction are used under CC-BY-4.0 with attribution; neither is redistributed in our repository.
  • Our own capture is personal traffic and is not redistributable; every finding derived from it is reproducible on any capture the reader controls.
  • No patent is claimed. The contribution we would defend is the measurement and the method, both of which are more valuable published than held.

16.4 Data protection

The sensor processes traffic metadata, not content, and writes no payload to disk. Evidence bundles contain feature vectors, decisions and hashes; they do not contain packet contents. Nothing is transmitted outward, which is a structural rather than a policy guarantee: the detection path cannot open a socket, and a test enforces it.

17.1 Who benefits, and how

17.2 National and sustainable-development alignment

  • Atmanirbhar Bharat and Make in India: no foreign cloud dependency, no outbound telemetry, no recurring licence in foreign currency.
  • Digital India: strengthens the trust layer beneath public digital infrastructure by protecting the networks that carry it.
  • SDG 9 (industry, innovation and infrastructure): protects the infrastructure on which industry depends.
  • SDG 16 (peace, justice and strong institutions): evidence that cannot be silently altered supports accountable investigation.

PART IV

Execution, limitations and conclusion

Chapter 18Project execution

18.1 How the work was organised

18.2 Working method

  • Predictions before runs. Every experiment file states what we expect before it is executed for the first time, and the run prints the verdicts.
  • A control for every claim. The discipline that cost us our headline claim (condition G) is the same discipline that makes the surviving claims credible.
  • Tune on the metric you report. A companion project of ours violated this and published a result that was wrong in its own favour's opposite direction; the lesson is applied here by reporting operating-point metrics alongside AUC.
  • Record every knob in the results payload, so a published row can be regenerated by the script that produced it.
  • Correct errors that ran against us, not only the flattering ones.

Chapter 19Limitations and future scope

19.1 Limitations, in full

  • 1 Gbps is not reached. Measured throughput is 610 to 672 Mbps.
  • Packet-size and timing sequence features are not implemented, although the problem statement names them beside fingerprints. This is the clearest remaining gap and is priority one.
  • Dictionary-based DGA families are weak (AUC 0.69 to 0.75).
  • Evidence integrity depends on a key held in the enclave; there is no external anchor or asymmetric signature yet.
  • No authentication or authorisation on the console: a recorded scope decision that assumes an already-restricted enclave.
  • Sharded output is not bit-exact: 8 to 21 cells per configuration differ from a single process.
  • Evaluation support is thin for two heads (13 test cells for exfiltration, 53 for DGA).
  • Tested on public corpora and our own capture, not yet on a vendor diode or a live critical-infrastructure network.
  • 1-RTT QUIC payloads remain out of reach, and always will be without keys; only the Initial handshake is analysed.

19.2 Roadmap

Chapter 20Conclusion

Threat detection behind a one-way link does not have to be a weaker copy of ordinary detection. On 877,801 real flows, a sensor that keeps sixteen aggregates of per-host behaviour over a sixty-second window scores 0.9810 binary F1 on one-way traffic, where a conventionally trained detector on the same tap falls to 0.6903 and a full two-way model reaches 0.9793. The constraint that looked like the problem - the missing direction - turned out not to be the cause of the loss at all.

Around that measurement we built a complete system: six detector heads covering the threat classes the problem statement names, severity separated from confidence, conformal abstention for the cases where an unverifiable guess is worse than silence, tamper-evident evidence that an analyst re-derives in an air-gapped browser, and an architecture whose read-only guarantee is enforced by its own build. It runs on a commodity server, carries no licence fee, and sends nothing outward.

We also measured its limits, and we report them in the same voice as its strengths: 610 to 672 Mbps rather than the 1 Gbps we once claimed; dictionary-based generated domains that our DNS features cannot separate; an evidence guarantee that a stolen key would void; two heads evaluated on very few cases. Seventeen of our forty-two pre-registered predictions were refuted, including the claim this project began with, and all seventeen are printed in this report.

That last point is the one we would ask an evaluator to weigh. A system whose authors can show which of their own beliefs the evidence destroyed is a system whose surviving claims mean something. On a network with no return path, where no one can tell the sensor it is wrong, that is the only kind of claim worth deploying.

Appendix CReproduction guide

Everything in Part II can be regenerated from the repository. Datasets are not redistributed: they are third-party and large.

cd ekagra/backend
pip install -e .

python -m pytest tests/ -q                     # 290 tests
python experiments/exp04_forward_features.py   # the headline ablation
python experiments/exp10_low_rate_diffuse.py   # the stress test
python experiments/exp11_dga_real_benign.py --capture <file.pcapng>
python demo.py                                 # API + console on :8000
python analyse_pcap.py <capture.pcapng>        # packet path on a capture
  • Place the corrected CIC-IDS2017 re-extraction (Zenodo 22016274) under backend/data/.
  • Each experiment prints its pre-registered predictions with verdicts and writes them to backend/results/exp*_verdicts.json.
  • The console also runs with no server: open frontend/index.html directly and it uses the bundled snapshot.
  • Figures in this report are produced by experiments/make_figures.py and by submission/ekagra_report/figures.py.

Appendix DEvidence bundle schema

{
  "seq": 90394,
  "ts": 1725638400.0,
  "threat_class": "ddos",
  "decision": "ALERT",            // or ABSTAIN
  "confidence": 1.0,              // conformal, per class
  "severity": {"level": "high", "score": 0.70},
  "observed": {"window": 59, "host": "105.35.144.90",
               "flows": 1, "peers": 0},
  "features": { ... 16 host-window + 9 protocol values ... },
  "model": "ba23cefcd9789cecc...",   // fingerprint of the deciding model
  "decision_path": [ ... ],
  "prev_hash": "b2882319284cd5ed...",
  "entry_hash": "5450847e8565c8d7...",  // SHA-256 of the canonical form
  "hmac": "5644012b36402abdc356..."     // HMAC-SHA256, key held in enclave
}
  • entry_hash covers the canonical form of every field above it, including prev_hash, which is what makes the record a chain rather than a list.
  • Severity is deliberately not hashed: it is a pure function of threat_class and features, both already committed, so hashing it would add a field that can never disagree while invalidating every record written before it existed.
  • Canonical form fixes key order and float precision, rejects non-finite values, and treats negative zero as zero (Ch 7.2).

Appendix EThe pre-registered prediction register

Forty-two predictions across ten experiments; seventeen refuted. The refuted set is listed in full in Chapter 9.7 with outcomes. The register below is the summary by experiment, as printed by the runs themselves into results/exp*_verdicts.json.

Appendix FAnticipated questions

Why not simply deploy Suricata or Zeek behind the diode?
They can run passively, but a large share of signatures and analysers depend on server responses, and rule updates require the network path the enclave does not have. We measured what losing the replies costs a trained detector: 0.9793 to 0.6903 binary F1.
Your 0.98 looks too high for CIC-IDS2017, which is a flawed dataset.
We use the corrected re-extraction, exclude source and destination addresses, and split temporally. We also publish the experiment that breaks our own number: under low-rate diffuse attacks, host-window-alone falls to 0.28 macro F1.
Is this not just XGBoost with extra steps?
The model is deliberately standard. The contribution is what it is fed (visibility-matched host-window state), what it refuses to say (calibrated abstention), and what it can prove afterwards (sealed evidence).
What does an abstention mean operationally?
It means the evidence available to this sensor does not support a confident label. It is 9.11% of cases, they are logged rather than dropped, and a rising rate is the drift signal a diode deployment otherwise has no way to receive.
What exactly does the evidence chain prove?
That no alert was edited, deleted or reordered after sealing - including by the operator - unless the HMAC key was stolen. That single exception is stated in the threat model rather than glossed over.
672 Mbps is not 1 Gbps. Is that a failure?
It is a measured gap that we state openly, having retracted our own earlier 1 Gbps claim. Sharding reaches 108,938 packets per second; line rate at 700-byte packets needs 178,571. A compiled fast path is the route, and it is on the roadmap rather than in the results.
How do you know the sensor is genuinely read-only?
A test parses every module in the detection path and fails the build if any network client is imported. The guarantee is enforced by the build, not asserted in a document.
What is the biggest technical weakness?
Packet-size and timing sequence features are not implemented, and the problem statement names them. Second is dictionary-based DGA, where AUC falls to 0.69.
What is the business risk you worry about most?
Procurement timelines. The zero-licence core is designed partly to let a pilot proceed without a purchase decision, so that technical value can be demonstrated before commercial commitment.
Why should an evaluator trust these numbers?
Because we publish the ones that went against us. Seventeen of forty-two pre-registered predictions were refuted, including the claim the project began with, and the verdicts are written by the experiment runs rather than by us.
